caption:
Did Wardenclyffe Tower ever work?

Nikola Tesla built the station at Shoreham, New York, in 1901–1902, on 200 acres bought from land developer James S. Warden. He intended to send messages, telephony and even facsimile images across the Atlantic to England and to ships at sea — not by radio waves, which he doubted existed, but by injecting current into the Earth itself and letting it resonate.

J. P. Morgan signed a contract in March 1901 for $150,000, taking a 51% interest in the company and its wireless patents. In June 1901 Tesla read an article by Marconi and concluded his earth-resonance system was being copied. He decided to scale the plant up, add wireless power delivery, and asked Morgan for much more money. Morgan refused and demanded an account of what had been spent.

Under the 186-foot tower was a wood- and steel-lined shaft sunk 120 feet, with a stairway inside. Tesla testified that machines at the bottom pushed iron pipes — he thought sixteen of them — three hundred feet outward, "to have a grip on the earth so the whole of this globe can quiver." Descriptions also mention four 100-foot tunnels radiating north, south, east and west, ending in small brick igloos.

On July 14, 1903, Morgan wrote that he would make no further advances. That night, and several nights after, newspapers reported the tower shooting off bright flashes that lit the sky. No explanation came from Tesla or his workers, and Wardenclyffe never seemed to operate again. The project was abandoned in 1906. On July 4, 1917, the Smiley Steel Company dynamited the tower for scrap; it took until September to bring it down, and the scrap realized $1,750.

What is still unresolved: how Tesla intended to combine the ground-conduction and atmospheric parts of his design is unknown. The purpose of the tunnels is only speculated — drainage, access, or improving the ground connection or resonance. The night flashes were never explained. And although Tesla lit lamps wirelessly at Colorado Springs, he did not scientifically test his theory; he believed he had achieved Earth resonance, which by his own theory would work at any distance.

cards.headline: He <y>doubted radio waves existed</y>, so he used the ground
cards.note: Tesla discarded Hertzian waves, believing they would travel straight out into space and be "hopelessly lost". Instead he theorized that current injected into the Earth at the right frequency would resonate in standing waves that could be tapped anywhere on the planet.
cards.source: Diagram from U.S. patent 1,119,732, Sheet 1, by Nikola Tesla — public domain
cards.alt: Line-drawn patent diagram sheet showing coils, a tower and grounding connections.

cards.headline: Morgan paid $150,000. Then Tesla <y>changed the plan</y>
cards.note: The March 1901 contract gave Morgan a 51% interest in the company and in the wireless patents. After reading a Marconi article that June, Tesla decided to scale up to a far more powerful transmitter with wireless power delivery — and asked for much more money. Morgan refused. This photograph was taken so Tesla could go back and ask again.
cards.source: File:Wardenclyffe Tower - 1904.jpg, 1904 — unknown author, public domain
cards.alt: The completed Wardenclyffe tower with its domed top, photographed above the brick laboratory.

cards.headline: A shaft 120 feet down, then <y>sixteen iron pipes</y>
cards.note: Tesla's 1923 foreclosure testimony describes a wood and steel lined shaft sunk 120 feet beneath the tower with a stairway inside. Machines at the bottom pushed iron pipes — he thought sixteen — three hundred feet out, so "the current through these pipes takes hold of the earth". Four 100-foot tunnels are also described, running north, south, east and west.
cards.source: Detail, U.S. patent 1,119,732 diagram by Nikola Tesla — public domain
cards.alt: Close detail of a patent drawing showing the grounding terminal and hatched earth line.

cards.headline: The night Morgan said no, <y>the tower lit the sky</y>
cards.note: Morgan's refusal letter came on July 14, 1903. That night and several nights after, newspapers reported bright flashes from the tower. Wardenclyffe never seemed to operate again. In 1917 the Smiley Steel Company dynamited it for scrap worth $1,750.
cards.source: File:Wardenclyffe tower tesla new york demolition july september 1917.png — attributed to the American Press Association, 1917, public domain
cards.alt: The tower tilted and broken apart mid-demolition, timbers splayed over open ground.

cards.headline: Nobody explained the flashes. Nobody <y>tested the theory</y>
cards.note: How Tesla meant to combine ground conduction with his charged-atmosphere method is unknown. The tunnels are still only speculated about: drainage, access, or improving the ground connection and resonance. He lit lamps wirelessly at Colorado Springs but never scientifically tested his Earth resonance claim. A rumour that the US government destroyed the tower over German spies was false — but Tesla had hidden the mortgages, so he could not say why it really came down.
cards.source: File:Wardenclyffe Tower.jpg, circa 1902 — author not recorded, public domain
cards.alt: Upper timber framing of the unfinished tower against pale sky, cupola not yet begun.
